sections.COMMENTS:
This Source straddles the southern side of the Sila Massif (called "Sila Piccola") in central Calabria. The Sila Massif is a mountainous plateau that reaches 1500 m above sea level and that overlies the Ionian subduction (Faccenna et al., 2005). This source is a W-dipping normal fault located east of the main extensional axis that runs along the southern Apennines.
Historical catalogues (Guidoboni et al., 2007; Rovida et al., 2016) show a remarkable concentration of damaging earthquakes around this area. As a matter of fact, these Calabrian earthquakes are among the strongest in Italy's long seismic history (Guidoboni et al., 2007; Rovida et al., 2016). In particular, the western region of the Sila Massif has been struck by the 27 March 1638 event (Mw 7.1; Calabria centrale), the eastern region by the 8 March 1832 (Mw 6.7; Crotonese), and the southern region by the 28 March 1783 (Mw 7.0; Calabria centrale). Concerning the 8 June 1638 (Mw 6.8; Crotonese) earthquake, and based on the study of Galli and Bosi (2003), we maintain that its epicenter lies within the Sila Piccola Massif, shifted westward respect to the macroseismically derived one. Our degree of knowledge on macroseismic effects of the 8 June 1638 event is limited because of the Sila mountainous and uninhabited region. This may have resulted in an intensity pattern of the June 1638 earthquake only partially complete, and hence in the mislocation of its epicenter.
Instrumental catalogues (e.g. ISIDe Working Group, 2016) show a scattered distribution of intermediate seismicity (Mw ca. 4) having depths ranging between 10 and 20 km in the Sila Massif, e.g. 13 July 1958 (Mw 4.6), 24 April 1991 (Mw 4.0), 5 April 2002 (Mw 4.2), 8 April 2008 (Mw 4.1), and 3 August 2015 (Mw 4.0) events.
This Source is a normal fault dipping toward the west. It is interpreted as a result of a south-eastward roll-back of the hinge of the subducting Ionian lithosphere causing extensional collapse of the orogenic belt (see Tiberti et al., 2017 for a summary). The overall role and geometry of this source is mostly based on review and geological data of Galli and Bosi (2003). This source model does not agree - at first glance - with the available damage pattern of the 8 June 1638 event (Guidoboni et al., 2007; Rovida et al., 2016) but, according to Galli and Bosi (2003), we maintain that it can be responsible for this mislocated earthquake.
This fault is considered active based on morphotectonic analyses (Galli and Bosi, 2003), and on contemporary historical reports describing a 60 miles-long fracture opened during the 8 june 1638 earthquake (D'Orsi, 1640; Di Somma, 1641; Paragallo, 1689).
The historical description of the surface faulting suggests even a 80 cm vertical offset (Di Somma, 1641). The location, offset and continuity of the fracture reported by all eye witnesses is a detailed, self-consistent and robust description of the surface faulting, and the persistence of the offset after 60 years (Martire, 1704) corroborate this view (Galli and Bosi, 2003). The fault has been studied by means of paleoseismological investigation that identified evidence of the June 1638 surface faulting plus four previous paleoearthquakes, and evaluated slip rates (Galli and Bosi, 2003; Galli and Scionti, 2006). A geochemistry survey was carried out cross the Ampollino Lake fault to investigate the gas bearing properties of the fault, and the migration processes of deep fluids (Sciarra et al., 2015).
This extensional fault is bounded to the north by a major transverse strike-slip structure known as Vette Line (Auct.; e.g. Moretti, 2000).
The strike was taken from the general orientation of mapped lineaments (e.g. Molin et al., 2004). The dip was inferred from regional geological considerations. The rake was assumed to represent pure extensional fault, inferred from geological and tectonic considerations. The minimum and maximum depth was based on surface geology and inferred from geological and seismological considerations, respectively. The slip rate was inferred from geodynamic constaints.
